title: Education, Press and Administrative Changes

cards.b: British rule built institutions that still run India: civil services, courts, police, schools, a free-ish press. It did so to serve empire. UPSC asks you to weigh both sides.

Lord Cornwallis, “father of the civil services”, separated revenue and justice, raised pay and created a covenanted service. The steel frame was the ICS. Police: district superintendent system (Cornwallis), Police Act 1861. Army: mostly Indian sepoys with British officers; recruitment later shifted to the “martial races” after 1857. Judiciary: Cornwallis Code (1793), the codification of laws by Macaulay (Law Commission 1833), High Courts Act 1861.

Entry by exam in London from 1855 (Indian Civil Service). Satyendranath Tagore was the first Indian in 1863. Age limit was cut to 19 in 1878 to keep Indians out. Indianisation was demanded by the Congress from 1885; simultaneous exams in India began only in 1922. The Lee Commission (1923 to 24) recommended direct recruitment, with 40% Europeans, 40% Indians direct and 20% promoted.

• Charter Act 1813: Rs 1 lakh yearly for education.
  • Orientalist–Anglicist debate: Macaulay’s Minute (1835) backed English; Bentinck accepted it.
  • Wood’s Despatch (1854): “Magna Carta of English education”; universities at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857); departments of education; grants-in-aid; vernacular primary schools.
  • Hunter Commission (1882): primary and secondary education.
  • Sadler Commission (1917 to 19): universities.
  • Hartog Committee (1929): primary education.

Macaulay wanted an English-educated class to “filter” knowledge down to the masses. It never worked. Literacy was about 12% in 1947. Female and rural education lagged. Yet the English-educated class gave rise to the nationalist leadership and to reformers. Colleges also taught ideas of liberty and nation that were turned against the Raj.

1780: Hickey’s Bengal Gazette, India’s first newspaper.

  • Censorship Act 1799 (Wellesley).
  • Metcalfe freed the press in 1835 (the “liberator of the press”).
  • Licensing Act 1857.
  • Vernacular Press Act 1878 (Lytton) — repealed 1882 by Ripon.
  • Newspaper (Incitement to Offences) Act 1908; Indian Press Act 1910.
Tilak’s Kesari and Mahratta, Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu and Bombay Chronicle were nationalist voices.

Regulating Act of 1773 set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta. Equal law was claimed, but there were separate courts for Europeans (the Ilbert Bill row of 1883, which gave Indian judges power over Europeans, was withdrawn in a diluted form). Sedition (S.124A) was added in 1870. The Arms Act 1878 disarmed Indians. Laws were written to protect the empire.

Colonial writers say that Britain gave India modern institutions. Nationalists such as Bipan Chandra reply that institutions were built to maintain the empire, and education was a means to produce clerks. Sumit Sarkar and others stress that Indians used these tools in their own ways. A balanced answer says: unintended gains, intended control.

The All India Services, the IPC (now replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, in force 1 July 2024), the district collector and the police structure all trace back here. The sedition law is in debate; the Supreme Court in 2022 put S.124A on hold. The three-language question and English medium still run on the Macaulay legacy.
